title: Bendōwa 1 - Holding to Fixed Views
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett opens a five-week series on Dogen's essay Bendōwa, using the Waddell and Abe translation, and begins with a cold that kept Nomon from sleeping until trying Janet's advice to sleep propped up, which exposes Nomon's fixed views about what is needed for sleep. Nomon connects this to the line "not holding to fixed views" in the Metta Sutta and to Thich Nhat Hanh on suffering well. Then Nomon sketches Dogen's life and three kinds of truth: historical, mythic, and practical. The first two paragraphs of Bendōwa follow, with the Jijuyo Samadhi ("self-fulfilling enjoyment") and the line that the Dharma "is amply present in every person."

sentences.text: Good evening everybody.
It's been a while since I've gotten to do this.
Thanks for inviting me.
I was just realizing it's a slick trick: if we have a practice period and we have a Shuso, a head student who does all the teaching, I do less.
That was pretty good.
Thanks.
Do we have a little more light in this?
Thanks, Bernadette.
Oh, that's good.
Thanks.
I can have less reading glasses that way.
I'm feeling a lot better, but I've had a bit of a cold lately.
I rarely get sick, so I don't like to complain or anything.
The symptoms were really pretty mild.
During the day I hardly notice anything.
That way if you get busy, you don't notice too much.
But then in the evening it would just start up and I'd start coughing, little fits of coughing.
Then I would lie down and go to sleep okay, but then at one or two in the morning, like clockwork, uncontrollable fits of coughing.

I'd have to get up, leave Janet in peace, go to the other room and just prop myself up somewhere and read or watch some TV or something until I got so exhausted that I could imagine going back to sleep.
I'd sleep a couple of hours and then it's time to get up.
So I was pretty tired.
But it wasn't really the cold, it was this losing sleep at night.
And it was weird though.
Why would the cold think anything different was going on at 2 a.m. versus 2 p.m.?
I didn't know how the cold was figuring that out.
Then Janet reminded me that when she has a cough, she always sleeps propped up and it helps her cough less.
I hadn't thought of that.
But then I thought, well, that won't work for me, because I know what I need to go to sleep.
I have to have just the right kind of pillows, and I lie on my side or my stomach, and it's been exactly the way it's been for a while.
Ever since one time when I dislocated my shoulder, I had to rearrange the way I slept, and now I have this arrangement and that's what works.
But after a few nights of this, I thought, what the hell?
I'll follow Janet's advice and try propping up to sleep.
I made a little throne for myself with pillows for my arms.
I just tried to relax and not tell myself too much that this isn't going to work.
And what do you know, I slept great.
So it's funny, isn't it, that we have these fixed views about who we are and what works for us, like all these internal rules.
I discovered I had these fixed views about what I need to go to sleep, which turned out not to actually be true.

Towards the end of the Metta Sutta that we chant at noontime, there's a classic Buddhist line, a philosophy line, that says, *not holding to fixed views.* So it would be nice to be reminded that we create so much suffering for ourselves and others holding these fixed views.
It's a fundamental idea in Buddhism that you don't have to do that.
It's not exactly our fault.
We're conditioned to do that, everyone's doing it, and we want to get in on it.
Everyone wants to have fixed views.
It's how we define ourselves.
But maybe we don't have to do that so much, because Buddhism is really ultimately about freedom.
Freedom from suffering, or maybe it's more accurate to say freedom in suffering, because there's going to be suffering, there's going to be pain.
And there can be no joy without suffering.
I was reading a lovely little piece by Thich Nhat Hanh, who's no longer actively teaching.
He can't really speak anymore.
Apparently he's doing okay, as best they can tell.
So now the Buddhist presses are going to keep republishing what he said for the next century, which is good.
Anyway, a little piece by Thich Nhat Hanh where he says:
*The art of happiness is also the art of knowing how to suffer well.
If we know how to use our suffering, we can transform it and suffer much less.
Knowing how to suffer well is essential to realizing true happiness.*
So that's true, isn't it?
I had to learn how to suffer much better with this cold, be a lot more skillful with it.
Another way of thinking about fixed views is that we are nothing but a bundle of fixed views.
Our very identity and our idea of who we are may just be a constellation, an ever-changing constellation, of fixed views.
So maybe we can really have a lot less suffering if we learn how to have fixed views in a good way.
Sometimes you can let them go because the evidence is there.
Other times, maybe we can be with our fixed views with more gentleness, more patience, more kindness, a little sense of humor.
We're pretty funny.
Although it's not too funny when we're enraged and lashing out at each other.
This doesn't mean that we don't have values.
Values and views are a little bit different.
We can have deep, important values about kindness, about love, about how things should be in our world, in our society.
But values are a lot more flexible, because values understand that situations are endlessly complicated and ever-changing.
And values inspire us to inquire in each moment, how should I express this value?
One moment the value of peace and harmony can be expressed one way, another moment that value might be expressed a very different way.
But views are fixed, right?
Views are like, it should be this way.
They should elect a fill-in-the-blank.
They should not do that.
They should do this.
So I think even when we want to be active in the world, which of course we do, fixed views probably don't really help us.
They just make us rigid and often make us angry.
So I was really grateful to have the right conditions to think about this in a fairly innocuous way.
I mean, it would have eventually been a problem if I kept not sleeping half the night for too many more nights.
But really it's a pretty mild problem.
So I'm really grateful when I have mild problems.
Aren't you glad?
It's good to have mild problems, because then we can study and we can learn.
These are teachings for us.
A great proponent of letting go of our views and our lineage is the great Zen master Dogen.
And we just chanted his name.
I don't know if you caught that going by.
Our first ancestor in Japan, great teacher Eihei Dogen or something.
He goes by a couple of different names.
Some traditional Zen characters have a million different names and it's hard to keep straight.
But Dogen will get you through the night with this guy.
Sometimes called Dogen Zenji.
Zenji is an honorific.
Sometimes called Eihei Dogen, which is naming him after the temple he founded.
Sometimes called Dogen Kigen.
I never could find out what Kigen means.
Maybe it's a family name, or maybe an earlier Dharma name.
But he has a thing or two to teach us about views.
And so the practice committee decided late last year we might focus a little bit on Dogen this year.
This is the beginning of that.
I'm going to give a series of talks in the next five weeks on one text of Dogen's called Bendowa.
So tonight we'll meet his essay called Bendowa.

And then on the weekend of May 20 and 21 we'll spend the weekend studying his great teaching Tenzo Kyokun, which is instructions for the head cook, in which he gets a little more practical and tells us how to cook.
But of course there's a lot to it from Dogen's point of view.
Cooking is not just cooking.
So that's our plan.
And then in July Edie's going to coordinate a cadre of sangha teachers to look at a bunch of little excerpts of Dogen's many, many different writings.
And there'll be a text we can all get.
The particular translation of this short essay called Bendowa that I'm using is from this book by Norman Waddell and Masao Abe.
I worked on making a photocopy but I haven't copied it yet.
So next week I'll bring you a copy of the text if you want to stick around and read it together.
And it's fine to not ever do that.
Just listen to the talks.
There's plenty.
But if you want to engage with it like study material, we'll have that available.
So it's interesting.
Dogen is such an important teacher to us.
He has a certain sensibility and a feeling for the practice.
Suzuki Roshi was a big Dogen fan, and Suzuki Roshi's way of understanding Dogen has really affected and formed the way we are.
The other Japanese priests who Suzuki Roshi brought over were interested in studying Dogen, Katagiri Roshi for one.
And then the American teachers who emerged have followed in this lineage and [unclear: "are guiding teacher for another week or two"].
Norman Fischer is a great fan of Dogen's.
He wrote a master's thesis on Dogen.
Did you know that?

Dogen is notoriously a little difficult to read, because he recognized that language and the concepts that language engenders are really limiting, and that we can't see the whole of the cloth with language.
But language is what we've got.
Language is what we have to communicate and describe and think.
So Dogen was very tricky and free and experimental with his language.
Even if he had been writing in English, which he was not, it would probably be quirky and interesting and hard to figure out what he means.
But he was writing in a combination of 13th century Japanese, which is different from modern Japanese, and Chinese, and not exactly the Chinese that the Chinese people would write.
It's the Chinese that the educated Japanese elite would study, which is a different version of Chinese.
So there are all these layers of language here.
And so translators into English find it really interesting and really challenging.
There's a whole little crew of them and they all know each other.
They get together and have conferences and complain and get excited and quibble over one little word, one little phrase.
One of our regional teachers, Peter Levitt, is a part of that cadre.

Another great source for Dogen studies is the huge work that he and Kazuaki Tanahashi put together, where they translated the major collection of Dogen's essays called Shobogenzo, which means Treasury of the Dharma Eye or the True Dharma Eye.
We have a copy of their great book in the library.
But for this I want to use these guys, because they've got better footnotes.
It makes it easier for me to look smart.
It makes it easier to study the text for all of us.
Kaz and Peter took on the task of doing this enormous volume, so they spent less time on footnotes.
These guys have spent a lot.

Actually, this book was published in 2004 or 2002, but the actual translation of Bendowa they originally published in a Buddhist journal in 1970-something, and then they've revised it every few years since, so they've been working on this for a while.
Lots of footnotes.

So anyway, Dogen lived from 1200 to 1253, and he was unusual as Zen masters go in that he really loved to write and loved to express himself in writing, both writing out his talks and then delivering them, which wasn't that common and still is not that common.
Norman likes to write out his talks, so I learned that from him, but I have many colleagues who don't write out their talks.
They just show up and say something.
And he would write his talks out, and he would also simply write essays and long letters.
We have in our chant book that you have there two of his texts.
One is the first thing he wrote that we know of, a little manual of meditation called Fukanzazengi.
The text I want to introduce to you tonight is the second text he ever wrote.
And then the other text that's in our chant book is called Genjokoan.
Actually, it was a long letter he wrote to a lay student, which I'm sure he revised and tinkered with after that.
So he wrote an enormous amount of stuff trying to express his sense of how Dharma really lives and breathes and really helps us.
His life story is a historic life story, and we all like that.
So that's maybe part of why he's considered the first ancestor and the great founder.
I think founders, when they're founding things, don't really think they're founding something.
At least that's my experience.
You just show up, try to do what you're doing, do your best.
I doubt he thought, I am founding a great new school of Buddhism or anything like that.
I think he was just like, okay, I'm back from China.
He did a famous epic journey to China as a young man because he wasn't quite satisfied with the Buddhism he encountered in Japan.
I think he got back and just put one foot in front of the next.
Originally he went back to the temple he had last practiced at in Kyoto, a place called Kenin-ji, which some of us have been to.
Then he found some little used temples a little outside of town to set up shop.
And then eventually he moved to a monastery out in the mountains called Eiheiji.
So I think we'll do bits and pieces of his life story in each of the talks.
Maybe that's more or less enough for tonight.
We don't really know with any certainty that much about exactly what he did besides the evidence from his writing.
The handy thing about his writings is he would write at the end when he wrote it and where.
So mostly the scholars say he can only really accurately be tracked through his writings.
One major piece of evidence is a journal that he wrote about his time in China as a young man.
But the problem is that journal was discovered after he died, in handwriting slightly different from his other work.
So scholars aren't really sure he wrote that.
It might have been one of his students who wrote it, either retelling stories that he had said or writing their own stories.
And there's a very detailed biography of Dogen written in the 15th century.
But do the math, that's 200 years later.
It includes all kinds of quotations of things that he said and things that he thought.
So who really knows?
But these historic stories are also helpful and useful to us.
When I think about original texts, I think about three levels of truth, and all three of them I think are really helpful, so we don't get too unbalanced.
The first truth is the first one we think about now, which is historical truth.
Like, what actually really happened?
We have this idea that there's something that really happened and other things that are made up, and there's only one really-happened thing.
Of course that's a little doubtful, right?
If you just compare notes with somebody you were hanging out with yesterday, you have different things that really happened.
But there is a sense of historicity, and that's real and valid.
So there's a kind of historic truth.
Historic truth matters, and it's interesting.
And then there's a devotional truth or a religious truth, and that was the first truth that Zen brought forward.

When we were first hearing, not me, when my predecessors were first hearing these stories about Dogen and about the Chinese ancestors, they were told by the teachers as if they actually, absolutely really happened that way.
It's a retelling of what's in the text and what's in the stories.
Dogen's life story was first told that way: first he did this, and then he had that thought, and he was concerned about this.
So that's a historic, a mythic truth, you could say.
Maybe mythic is better than devotional, because we don't want to be too devoted to anything, but too bad for us.
We're in a devotional practice.
We thought it was very rational when we signed up, and it turns out to be very devotional and about love, actually.
So there's a historic truth.
There's a devotional or a mythic truth, where you just lose yourself in this stuff.
Why not have it be real?
Why not have it be true?
Just jump into it.
Walk along with Dogen as he's walking these dusty roads in China, a 20-year-old uppity young monk from Japan looking down his nose at various teachers until at last he finds his true teacher.
Hallelujah!
That's great.
That's wonderful.
So diving into it is a kind of devotional truth or mythic truth.
And the third truth is the practical truth.
Well, how do we actually practice with this?
What's useful to me here?
How can I bring this into my life?
And what's the point of any of it without that?
But I think we need all three.
So as we study different texts, it's good to touch on all three: historical, so-called real; devotional, like entering the story; and practical.
What's here for me?
How can I work with this?
One thing that's a little slippery about practical truth, though, is that with this stuff you have to really evaluate the practicality carefully.
You have to let that practicality inhabit you in a slow-burn kind of way.
Sometimes we're too quick, right?
Because that's our mode.
We reject all kinds of stuff: "Oh, no, that's not for me."
Right?
Fixed views are back.
So when examining the practical truth, you have to try stuff on, really wear it for a while, walk around in it, breathe with it, check it out.
So that's part of why I think it's great to study these texts of Dogen and other people: because they're difficult.
It's good that they're difficult.
How did easy work out?
So that's my little preface about the text and about Dogen.

This was written in 1231, and the title, Ben Do Wa, is four Chinese characters together, which one of the translators I looked at said in his footnote, yeah, but the problem is that, three characters, sorry, three characters, but he said these three characters actually aren't usually put together.
Chinese characters are interesting: each one has a meaning by itself, and they have meanings in combination.
But it more or less means entering the way, negotiating the way, celebrating the way, being in the way.
The Do in the middle is unambiguous.
That's the Do like Zen, like Kendo, Kyodo, in all the different ways, right?
There's a ton of them.
So the way is unambiguous, but the Ben and the Wa are a little bit ambiguous.
More or less it means entering the way.
Since he was born in 1200, he was about 31 when he wrote this, and it was like his opening salvo: here's my understanding, here's what I want to share with Japan.
At least that's the mythic truth of it.
The historical truth is it didn't go very far for quite a long time.
For one thing, very, very few texts were carved into the wooden blocks for printing.
There wasn't a whole lot of printing going on.
I'd be curious if anyone knows about printing, the state of printing in the Tokugawa era.
I didn't look that up, but I think very little stuff was printed.
So it was handwritten, and a few copies were made by hand.
But then the funny thing about Dogen's writing is that, even back then, he didn't have a ton of disciples.
He was not a hugely popular guy, but he had very devoted disciples, very devoted students who really treasured him.
And so his writing became like treasured artifacts.
And what do you do with a treasured artifact?
If you're a Japanese abbot, you lock it away.
So it was not like they were sent to the libraries.
They didn't have libraries, I don't think.
So Bendawa didn't go very far.
It was read by a few people.
I'm sure they gave talks using this material.
But it mostly sat in the treasure rooms of different monasteries in Japan.
I don't know how many copies there were, so a few.
Then there was a great revival of Dogen studies in the 18th century, and then it was printed and published.
Maybe they even had movable type by then or something, I don't know.
So here's the first paragraph of Bendawa.
*Buddha Tathagatas all have a wonderful means, unexcelled and free from human agency, for transmitting the wondrous Dharma and realizing supreme and complete awakening.
That this means is only passed directly from Buddha to Buddha without deviation is due to the Jijuyo Samadhi, which is its touchstone.*
So typical of Dogen, the whole idea is in the first paragraph.
The rest is just different ways of talking about it.
So let's hear that again, and I'll try to unpack it a little bit.
*Buddha Tathagatas*, so this is like the great Buddhas.

*All have a wonderful means*, a wonderful way, *unexcelled and free from human agency*, so unbound by human, beyond human, *for transmitting the wondrous Dharma and realizing supreme and complete awakening.

That this means is only passed directly from Buddha to Buddha without deviation is due to the Jijuyo Samadhi, which is its touchstone.* These translators left a word untranslated, because it's a tricky word, and other translators have all different ways of translating this key phrase.
That all of this flow and transmission of teachings is due to a certain way of practicing, a certain way of being, a kind of Samadhi called Jijuyo Samadhi.
Samadhi means concentration, and it's both a process and a result, all combined together.
It's a process of concentration, of focus, of awareness, and therefore also a way of being in the world with connectedness and groundedness.

In the traditional Mahayana texts, which I haven't particularly studied, I read that there are more than a hundred different kinds, many, many different ways to practice concentration, and all of this is supported by many different kinds of meditation.
So this is a particular concentration, a particular Samadhi that he's extolling, called the Jijuyo Samadhi.
Jijuyo is three characters, and I think the best translation I can think of so far is self-fulfilling enjoyment Samadhi.
Self-fulfilling enjoyment Samadhi.
We don't think of enjoyment right away when we think of Zen.
So maybe we should update our fixed views about that and let those go.
But this could be deeply about enjoyment, but a certain kind of enjoyment.
So, self-fulfilling.
Self-fulfilling does not mean like this self.
It's more like the Samadhi, the concentration, has its own self-efficacy.
It's more like self-driving cars.
It just knows how to take care of itself.
So it's a deeply fulfilling and enjoyable Samadhi.
The idea here is that it's one of many ways that Dogen talked about practice.
Interestingly, I asked my colleagues about this on the Zen priest email, the Zen teacher email.
It was really fun, because a lot of them are total Buddhist geeks and they could look stuff up in their Chinese dictionaries and stuff.
They said that this phrase is very rarely used.
It's used rarely in texts that Dogen had access to, but not very often.
So something about this phrase just caught Dogen's fancy early in his career.

And then he didn't use it very much after this either, which doesn't fit the linear narrative, like this was the beginning of his teaching, and now he will endlessly extol the virtues of Jiju's Samadhi.
He came up with other ways of talking, just like you would, right?
Just like any of us would.
So this rehumanizes Dogen, I think, for us.
Another main way that he expressed this idea is the phrase practice enlightenment.
In English it gets translated as a hyphenated phrase, practice-enlightenment, and in Japanese slash Chinese it's just a chunk of characters that he always put together.
The idea here is that we have a big fixed view that these teachings can help us with.
Our big fixed view is that we're kind of messed up, that we're a little bit broken, in need of improvement.
We tried all other kinds of improvement plans, and so now we've resorted to meditation, eventually.
And he's saying that that attitude is not the ultimate, deepest way we can approach our practice.
I think it's provisionally perfectly true that the practice of meditation has all the benefits we hope it will.
At least I assume that's why you're here.
Maybe it'll make us calmer and more grounded and less reactive and a little wiser, able to feel some quality of our life that's hard to access when we're spun up.
But Dogen's saying, no, there's a deeper truth here.
That deeper truth is that we're not broken.

That's a fixed view that we could let go of, that we could completely abandon by dropping deeply into the practice, by dropping deeply into the root feeling of human life, which is then even beyond human life: it is Buddha life.
There's an opening saying that this is about Buddhas, and it's beyond human agency, and it only passes from a Buddha to a Buddha.
The next paragraph will help us a little bit, so I'll say a few words about that in a minute.
Let's see if I can say more about ji, jiu, and yu.
In the next paragraph he says, *to disport oneself freely*, to practice or play freely.
Disport has an element of play in it.
So here's play.
You enjoying it?
Play.
*To disport oneself freely in this samadhi, the right entrance is proper sitting in zazen.* So now we know where we are again.
*The Dharma is amply present in every person, but without practice it is not manifested.
Without realization it is not attained.
It is not a question of one or many.
Let loose of it and it fills your hands.
It is not bounded vertically or horizontally.
Speak it and it fills your mouth.
Within this Dharma, Buddhists dwell everlastingly, leaving no perceptions in any sphere or direction.
All living beings use it unceasingly, with no sphere or direction appearing in their perception.*
So let's just do the first two sentences, and I'll say a little more about ji, jiu, and yu.
You may not realize it's about two minutes to the line.
Okay, thanks.
*To disport oneself freely in this samadhi, the right entrance is proper sitting in zazen.* So zazen matters, but it's not how we make it happen; it's the entrance.
It makes it a little more like a doorway.
We tend to think, what I need is inside that building, now I've got to go in there.
But maybe it's actually the doorway that matters, not what's inside the building.
And he says, we already have it.
*The Dharma is amply present in every person, but without practice it is not manifested, without realization it is not attained.*
And this next part is so beautiful.
Listen to this.
*It is not a question of one or many.
Let loose of it and it fills your hands.* So let it go and it fills your hands.
*It is not bounded vertically or horizontally.* That's code: vertical means your nose, and horizontal means your eyes.
So that's the senses.
It's not bounded by the senses.
It's not bounded by what you can see or smell or perceive.
It's beyond perception.
*Speak it and it fills your mouth.* All you have to do is speak it.
Just open your mouth and you'll be proclaiming the true Dharma.
*Within this Dharma, Buddhists dwell everlastingly,* and then a whole lot of other complicated stuff about perception.
So maybe I'll just close with a few more words about Ji, Ji and you, and then we'll call it a night.
Ji means itself.
That's the self-supporting part of it.
Ji means to receive.
It's the same Ji as in Jiu Kai.
So itself is being received.
Something is being received: the Dharma is being received.
And Ji means to employ something, to use something or to immerse yourself in something.
In terms of Ji and you, when you put them together, it means fulfilling.
There's a sense of fulfillment to receiving and using this thing that's already complete without you, that already knows how to take care of itself.
It doesn't need you, and yet you need it and it needs you.
You already have it, you're already complete, and yet you need to practice.
The later biographies of Dogen, some of the things that they said about Dogen, kind of putting words in his mouth, were that that's really what mystified Dogen.
Various teachers were telling him, these teachings, yeah, you're already like a Buddha.
You have the Buddha nature, you're already complete.
And memorize this text, learn this ritual, do that, get up there early, do this, do that, do that.
And he's like, well, why do we need to do all that if we're already complete?
And somehow he needed to go to a whole other land and have an epic journey.
It's like Homer.

Epic journey like Odysseus, and come back and somehow have a deeper feeling of what they were telling him all along: that *the Dharma is amply present in every person, but without practice it's not manifested.*
Okay, so that's a little beginning with Dogen.
Thanks.
Sorry I didn't leave you time for questions, but that's okay.
Your questions are already answered.
All right, but we'll have more time other weeks.
It's not a very long text, thankfully.
The bulk of it is just about five, six paragraphs, and then there's a whole bunch of extra stuff at the end that we'll just dip into.
*Equally extend to every*

verbatim.text: Good evening everybody. It's been a while since I've gotten to do this. Thanks for inviting me. So I was just realizing it's like a slick trick that if we have a practice period and we have a Shuso, you know, a head student who does all the teaching, I do less. That was pretty good. Thanks. Do you want more light? Yeah, do we have a little more light in this? Thanks, Bernadette. Oh, that's good. Thanks. I can have less reading glasses that way.

So I'm feeling a lot better, but I've had a bit of a cold lately. I rarely get sick, so I don't like to complain or anything. And the symptoms were really pretty mild. During the day, I hardly really know, I hardly notice anything. You know, that way if you get busy, you don't notice too much. But then in the evening, it would just kind of start up and I'd start coughing, little sort of fits of coughing. And then I would lie down and go to sleep okay,

but then like one or two in the morning, like clockwork, uncontrollable fits of coughing. Yeah. And then I'd have to get up, I'd leave, you know, leave Janet in peace go to the other room and just prop myself up somewhere and read or watch some TV or something until I got so exhausted that I could imagine going back to sleep, sleep a couple hours and then it's time to get up. So I was pretty tired. But it wasn't really the cold, it was this losing sleep at night.

And it was weird though, why would the cold think anything different was going on at 2 a.m. versus 2 p.m.? I didn't know how the cold was figuring that out. And then Janet reminded me that when she has a cough, she always sleeps propped up and it helps, you know, cough as much. I hadn't thought of that. But then I thought, well, that won't work for me because I know what I need to go to sleep. I have to have just the right kind of pillows and I line my side or my stomach and it's been exactly the way it's been for a while.

Ever since one time when I dislocated my shoulder, I had to kind of rearrange the way I slept and now I have this arrangement and that's what works, you know. But after a few nights of this, I thought, what the hell? I'll follow Janet's advice and try propping up to sleep. I kind of made a little throne for myself with pillows for my arms, you know. Just try to relax and try not to too much tell myself this isn't going to work. And what do you know, I slept great. So it's funny, isn't it, you know, that we have these fixed views

about who we are and what works for us, like all these internal rules. So I discovered I had these fixed views about what I need to go to sleep, which turned out not to actually be true. Towards the end of the Metta Sutta that we chant at noontime, there's a line, a classic Buddhist line, a philosophy line that says, not holding to fixed views.
